content.thinking:
I'm reviewing the io-shop account page failures: the legacy-checkout-fallback flag was switched off at 03:38:40 while monthly-spend-feature was switched on at the same moment. Reverting monthly-spend-feature is already ruled out, and turning legacy-checkout-fallback back on is confirmed as the fix, so the document treats that flag as the trigger. Next I'm tracing how the account page failures reached shoppers.

I'm tracing the causal chain for the account page failures: requests hit a ZeroDivisionError in the new renderer, which was serving the pages because legacy-checkout-fallback had been switched off at 03:38:40. I'm now weighing whether the monthly-spend-feature switch-on, which happened at that same instant, can be ruled out as an earlier cause.

I'm confirming that the monthly-spend-feature switch-on can't be the trigger: after reverting it didn't help and I put it back on, the service stayed healthy with it in place once legacy-checkout-fallback was restored. I'm also checking whether any deploy in the window could account for it, though the deploy reads so far came back empty.

I'm checking the reasoning about why switching off the fallback broke the account pages. The likely mechanism is that the new renderer fails for shoppers with no purchases this month, but that rests on one reading I haven't actually run yet, so I'm not treating it as settled.

I'm working out how the legacy-checkout-fallback switch-off sent account pages to the new renderer. With that flag off, the new path fails whether or not monthly-spend-feature is on, and with it on the pages are fine, so the fallback is what routed traffic there.

I'm working out the root cause now: with the legacy fallback off, account pages render the monthly spend summary, and its per-item average divides by a count that can be zero for shoppers with no purchases this month.

I'm checking how the cause would be described to a reader: switching off an older fallback sent account pages through a newer path that probably fails for shoppers who bought nothing this month, since it divides by that month's purchase count. I'm also considering the risk that turning the fallback off again would route pages back through that same renderer.

I'm now listing the contributing factors: no check was run on the flag-off path before the toggle, and both flags were flipped at the same instant straight to all traffic. A staged rollout would likely have caught the failure before most shoppers hit it.

I'm now sorting out the contributing factors, and I'm weighing whether the two flag changes landing at the same moment is itself a factor, since it may have pushed the investigation toward the wrong flag first.

I'm weighing a fourth contributing factor: the new renderer had no test for a shopper with no purchases this month, and I'm checking whether the fix's own tests already cover that case.

I'm turning to the action items now: a gradual rollout for io-shop flag changes that halts when errors rise, one flag changed at a time, and paging on-call for high error rates on the shop.

I'm weighing whether a missing test for shoppers with no purchases this month is a separate contributing factor, and I'm checking whether the fix's own tests already cover that case, which they do.

I'm listing what went well: Argus tried both flags in turn and put monthly-spend-feature back on when the revert didn't help, and the Mitigation Agent's revert of legacy-checkout-fallback restored the service. I'm also noting the Investigator's read of the flag changes, logs, and metrics, and the draft fix PR #550.

I'm checking whether the lead about the monthly-spend flag actually shaped the response: the Investigator dismissed it, and Argus reverted monthly-spend-feature first, so the flag it pointed to only got turned back on as the second candidate, which is what restored the service.

I'm leaving out the specific figures and file paths, and keeping the assumptions in view: the link between the legacy fallback flag and the renderer that serves account pages comes from the logs and the mitigation results, since no such flag appears in the repository. The claim that empty-month accounts are the ones failing also rests on that same earlier reading. For the symptom, I'll describe it simply as account page requests failing with errors, citing the error logs and the baseline error rate.

I'm laying out the causal steps now: account page requests failed with errors, the spend summary hit a division-by-zero, and the new renderer was serving those pages in place of the legacy one.

I'm settling on the last step of the causal chain: the new renderer's monthly per-item spend average divides by zero, which the code reading attributes to shoppers with no purchases this month. I also want a contributing factor noting that nothing checked whether the new renderer was safe before the fallback was switched off.

action_items.item: Roll out changes to io-shop feature flags gradually, with an automatic halt and revert when the error rate rises.
Require production flag changes on io-shop to be made one at a time, with a pause to watch errors between them.
Route the io-shop error-rate alert to the on-call rotation so that it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed far more often than before.
The failed requests broke on a division-by-zero error raised while the page's spend summary was being built.
The error came from the new renderer, which had started serving account pages that the legacy renderer had served until then.

ruled_out.what: The switch-on of the feature flag monthly-spend-feature at the same instant (P2): the service stayed at the incident's level with it turned off again, and it was back to normal with it on once the fallback was restored.

causal_chain.step: Pages moved to the new renderer because the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off.
The new renderer's monthly per-item spend average divides by zero, and the reading of the code puts this down to shoppers with no purchases this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off an older fallback sent shoppers' account pages through a newer way of building them, and that newer way likely breaks for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, because it divides by that month's number of purchases.

contributing_factors.factor: The legacy fallback was switched off for all account-page traffic at once. No check was seen that the path it exposed, the new renderer, worked first, and no staged rollout was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A gradual switch-off, halted on rising errors, would have stopped the failure while only a small part of shoppers had reached the new renderer.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Two feature flags were changed at the same instant, so the investigation could not tell their effects apart and blamed the wrong flag first.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Separate changes would have pointed straight at the fallback switch-off, so the first revert would have been the one that worked and the service would have recovered sooner.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen for the monthly spend average with a shopper who has bought nothing this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Such a test would have exposed the division by zero before the new renderer took account-page traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The error-rate alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An on-call person would have been engaged from the alert, ready to act on the thread's lead if the automated reverts had not restored the service.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done first: the investigation weighed it as refuted and Argus reverted monthly-spend-feature first, and the flag the lead named was switched back on only as the second candidate, which turned out to be the action that put the service back.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read the flag history, the logs and the metrics, and tied the errors to a division by zero in the new renderer.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back on when turning it off did not help, so the refuted action was not left in place.
The Mitigation Agent switched legacy-checkout-fallback back on, and that put the service back to normal.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request.

went_wrong: The Investigator weighed the thread's lead as refuted and ranked the monthly-spend-feature switch-on first, so the first revert targeted the wrong flag and the flag the lead named was restored only on the second try.

input.root_cause: Once account pages went through the new renderer, its monthly spend summary called average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the month's total by the number of purchases made this month and has no guard for an empty list. So it raises ZeroDivisionError for every shopper who has bought nothing this month, and serve_account_page turns that into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: Switching the legacy checkout fallback off again, or anything else that sends account pages to the new renderer, could make account pages fail again for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
